title: Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 24 Sep 2026]
    Title:Your Transformer Can Hold Two Thoughts at Once: Evidence of Linear Superposition in LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:While Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on highly non-linear components, in this work we demonstrate that they exhibit fundamental linearity: when inputs from distinct text streams are linearly combined, the model outputs a superposition of the individual next-token distributions. We term this the \textit{Superposition Linearity Hypothesis}. We provide evidence that superposition is an intrinsic property of the Transformer architecture rather than an emergent consequence of training; in fact, we observe that it tends to diminish as pretraining progresses. However, we demonstrate that linearity can be substantially restored through lightweight fine-tuning, significantly reducing the divergence between the predicted next-token distribution and the average of the individual next-token distributions. Finally, we introduce a guided decoding procedure that disentangles superposed outputs, enabling the simultaneous generation of two coherent continuations from a single forward pass.

report.summary: A new paper shows Transformers can linearly superpose two text streams, enabling a single forward pass to yield two coherent continuations.
report.background: Large language models are built from nonlinear components, so most research assumes their internal computations are highly nonlinear. Yet mechanistic interpretability has found evidence of linear structure in activation space, especially in the residual stream. This paper formalizes a Superposition Linearity Hypothesis: when two distinct text streams are linearly combined as input, the model's next-token distribution becomes a superposition of the individual distributions. The authors argue this is intrinsic to the Transformer architecture, not just a training artifact, and show it weakens during pretraining. They then restore linearity with lightweight fine-tuning and use guided decoding to separate the mixed signals.
key_points: The Superposition Linearity Hypothesis states that linearly combining two input streams makes the model output a weighted average of the next-token distributions for each stream. This suggests Transformers can process multiple 'thoughts' in parallel within one forward pass rather than strictly sequentially.

The effect appears to be an intrinsic property of the Transformer architecture, not an emergent skill learned from data. Interestingly, the paper reports that linear superposition tends to diminish as pretraining progresses, implying standard training may suppress this capacity.

Lightweight fine-tuning can substantially restore superposition linearity, sharply reducing the divergence between the superposed prediction and the average of individual predictions. This means practitioners may be able to recover parallel-stream behavior without full retraining.

A guided decoding procedure disentangles the superposed outputs, allowing simultaneous generation of two coherent continuations from a single forward pass. This could cut inference cost for dual-generation tasks and inspire new decoding strategies.

The findings connect mechanistic interpretability with practical efficiency: if models natively hold multiple linear signals, developers might exploit this for controllable, multi-task, or multi-perspective generation without duplicating compute.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this work could reframe inference efficiency: if one forward pass can produce and separate two streams, providers may reduce compute for parallel generation, comparison, or ensemble-like tasks. Developers gain a potential new primitive for guided decoding and model steering, especially if lightweight fine-tuning reliably restores linearity. Interpretability researchers get evidence that linear structure is architectural, deepening mechanistic understanding of residual streams. Regular users might see faster dual-response features, such as simultaneous draft and critique or two stylistic continuations from a single prompt. However, safety and alignment teams must consider whether superposed outputs make monitoring, attribution, and control harder, since one hidden state now encodes multiple latent continuations.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the paper's code release on GitHub and arXiv. Relevant tools include TransformerLens for activation analysis, nnsight for remote interpretability, Hugging Face Transformers for fine-tuning experiments, and PyTorch for custom guided decoding. Researchers can also use SAE-based libraries like dictionary_learning to probe linear features. For reproducing superposition tests, start with small open models such as GPT-2 or Pythia, then extend to instruction-tuned LLMs.
